payload.name: glottal-insufficiency
payload.scope: People made glottal-insufficiency to categorize the failure of vocal fold closure during phonation or airway protection so that clinicians can identify the gap morphology, its etiology, and select appropriate treatment.

definition.body: Glottal insufficiency is a clinical construct that maps the failure of the vocal folds to achieve complete closure during phonation or airway protection, resulting in abnormal airflow and voice quality. Parameters: (1) the gap morphology - anterior commissure gap, posterior glottic chasm, unilateral or bilateral fold bowing, or asymmetric closure; (2) the etiology - vocal fold paralysis or paresis, presbylaryngis-related atrophy, sulcus vocalis, surgical resection, or neurologic degeneration; (3) the functional consequences - breathy voice quality, glottal airway leak measured by aerodynamic flow, compensatory hyperfunction of supraglottic structures, and potential aspiration risk. It persists as a maintained diagnostic category in laryngology classification systems, documented in clinical assessment protocols and surgical planning documents. e.g.: breathy voice with posterior glottic gap in a patient with unilateral vocal fold paralysis; bilateral bowing seen in presbylaryngis; complete glottic incompetence following bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury | not: glottic stenosis, which narrows the airway by scarring rather than failure of fold closure; laryngomalacia, which is supraglottic collapse rather than glottic closure failure [formal: insufficientia glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Laryngeal motor disorder is a clinical construct that classifies conditions in which the neuromuscular control of the larynx is disrupted, producing abnormal voice, breathing, or swallowing. Parameters: (1) the motor pattern - hyperadductory, hypoadductory, or abductor failure; (2) the neurologic substrate - peripheral nerve injury (recurrent laryngeal nerve, superior laryngeal nerve), central nervous system lesion, peripheral neuropathy, or dystonic dysregulation; (3) the clinical phenotype - breathy voice from fold bowing, strained-strangled voice from spasm, breathiness on onset, or aspiration. It persists as a maintained classification in neurology and laryngology practice, documented in the Modified Neurologic Laryngology Scale and standardized assessment protocols. e.g.: adductor spasmodic dysphonia producing strained-strangled voice with glottic spasms; bilateral vocal fold paralysis from thyroid surgery damaging both recurrent laryngeal nerves; abductor spasmodic dysphonia causing inspiratory stridor | not: laryngeal-tumor, which is a structural mass lesion rather than a neuromuscular disorder; gastroesophageal-reflux, which causes laryngeal irritation without primary motor disruption [formal: disorder motorius laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Presbylaryngis is a clinical construct that categorizes the progressive atrophy and tissue remodeling of the larynx associated with aging, producing characteristic voice and aerodynamic changes. Parameters: (1) the structural changes - atrophy of the vocalis muscle, thinning of the lamina propria layers, increased Reinke space compliance loss, calcification of thyroid and cricoid cartilages; (2) the aerodynamic consequence - reduced maximum phonation time, increased glottal airway leak, decreased subglottal pressure efficiency; (3) the acoustic phenotype - breathy voice with increased jitter and shimmer, reduced vocal range, decreased maximum intensity. It persists as a maintained diagnostic category in geriatric laryngology, documented in the Geriatric Voice Assessment Protocol and clinical text descriptions of age-related voice change. e.g.: breathy voice with glottic gap in an 80-year-old patient with bilateral vocal fold atrophy; reduced maximum phonation time to 8 seconds in presbylaryngis without other pathology; voice change documented over 5-year follow-up in a patient with progressive vocal fold bowing | not: presbycusis, which is age-related hearing loss affecting voice monitoring but not the laryngeal structures themselves; spasmodic dysphonia, which is a dystonic motor disorder rather than age-related atrophy [formal: presbylaryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: glottal-airway-leak
payload.scope: People made glottal-airway-leak as a measured construct quantifying the volume of air escaping through the glottis during phonation, enabling objective assessment of vocal fold closure efficiency.

definition.body: Glottal airway leak is a clinical measure that quantifies the volume of air escaping through the glottis during attempted phonation, reflecting the degree of vocal fold closure insufficiency. Parameters: (1) the measurement method - aerodynamic flow measured by pneumotachograph or digital voice analyzer during sustained vowel phonation; (2) the normalized metric - glottal airflow rate expressed in milliliters per second or as a percentage of total expiratory airflow; (3) the clinical threshold - normal closure (below 100 ml/s), mild leak (100-300 ml/s), moderate leak (300-600 ml/s), severe leak (above 600 ml/s). It persists as a maintained measurement standard in laryngology practice, documented in clinical voice assessment protocols and instrumental evaluation guidelines. e.g.: sustained /a/ phonation showing 450 ml/s glottal leak in a patient with unilateral vocal fold paralysis; normal glottal airflow of 40 ml/s in a healthy voice; elevated leak of 720 ml/s during bilateral vocal fold paralysis; pre- and post-injection comparison showing reduction from 500 ml/s to 80 ml/s after vocal fold augmentation | not: nasopharyngeal leak, which measures air escaping through the nose during oral speech; cough airflow, which is a protective reflex measurement not a phonatory assessment [formal: fugacium viae glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: laryngeal-palpation
payload.scope: People made laryngeal-palpation to systematically assess the larynx through external hand contact, providing information about cartilage position, symmetry, and mobility that internal visualization cannot fully capture.

definition.body: Laryngeal palpation is a manual examination technique in which the clinician uses external finger pressure on the neck to assess the position, symmetry, mobility, and sensitivity of the laryngeal cartilages and surrounding structures. Parameters: (1) the palpation regions - thyrohyoid membrane, thyroid cartilage notch, cricothyroid space, cricoid cartilage, and the lateral soft tissues of the anterior neck; (2) the assessment targets - thyroid cartilage tilt and rotation, cricothyroid joint mobility, thyrohyoid distance change during phonation, subcutaneous emphysema, and tenderness or crepitus; (3) the clinical indications - suspected laryngeal trauma, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, laryngeal fracture, tracheoesophageal speech assessment, or preoperative airway evaluation. It persists as a maintained clinical skill in laryngology and otolaryngology training, documented in physical examination textbooks and clinical practice guidelines. e.g.: palpating the thyrohyoid membrane for increased tension during vowel phonation; assessing cricothyroid joint mobility by lateral finger pressure on the cricothyroid space; palpating the neck for crepitus following laryngeal trauma; subcutaneous emphysema on laryngeal palpation after laryngeal surgery [formal: palpatio laryngea | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: vocal-fold-augmentation
payload.scope: People made vocal-fold-augmentation to map the injectable materials and techniques used to medialize paralyzed or atrophic vocal folds, enabling comparison of biomaterials and clinical outcomes.

definition.body: Vocal fold augmentation is a clinical construct that categorizes injectable biomaterials and the procedural techniques used to increase the bulk of atrophic or paralyzed vocal folds, improving glottic closure and voice quality. Parameters: (1) the injectable material - autologous fat, calcium hydroxylapatite, carboxymethylcellulose gel, polytetrafluoroethylene paste, hyaluronic acid, or collagen; (2) the procedural route - percutaneous transthyroid injection under local or general anesthesia, direct laryngoscopic injection under microlaryngoscopy, or endoscopic injection with laryngeal nerve guidance; (3) the duration of effect - temporary (absorbed in weeks to months), intermediate (6-12 months), or permanent (fibrosis or integration). It persists as a maintained procedural category in phonosurgical practice, documented in the Voice Enhancement Consensus Statement and standardized laryngeal surgery textbooks. e.g.: percutaneous injection of calcium hydroxylapatite (Restylane) for unilateral vocal fold paralysis; fat graft medialization for presbylaryngis-related vocal fold atrophy; autologous fat augmentation in a patient with bilateral vocal fold atrophy following thyroid cancer resection | not: thyroplasty type I, which is a cartilage window implant rather than an injectable augmentation; botulinum-toxin-injection, which reduces muscle activity rather than adding bulk [formal: augmentatio plicae vocalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.note: Pinned sense: glottal-insufficiency is a specific type of laryngeal motor disorder characterized by failure of vocal fold closure. The laryngeal-motor-disorder construct classifies neuromuscular failures of the larynx producing abnormal voice; glottal-insufficiency is the hypoadductory subtype where the motor pattern is inadequate adduction. A competent clinician would call glottal insufficiency a type of laryngeal motor disorder - it is a failure of laryngeal motor function (inadequate adduction). The nearest accepted kind is laryngeal-motor-disorder, which is broader and includes hyperadductory and abductor patterns as well. [Law 9]
